en: The śramaṇa Ji composed this treatise.

Having extensively analyzed [the preceding sections] up to the "basis of the two divisions," he states: From the following verse onward, there is a formal explanation of the transformation of consciousness.
Within this, first, the preceding section is concluded and the subsequent question is posed; next, the verse is cited as the answer.
As it is said in the verse of the first fascicle:
"This transformative consciousness consists of only three types:
namely, the maturation, the deliberation, and..."
And the consciousness that discerns objects—
these briefly set forth the three types of self-transforming entities. In the second volume, following the verse on the *ālaya*,
the self-natures of these three transformations are explained in detail.
And there are the seeing and image aspects.
This is because the seeing and image aspects are transformations of the self-substance aspect;
they are the functions of the self-substance aspect.
It is stated that the self-substance (*svabhāva*) is the basis for the two divisions.
This concludes the three lines of verse from the first fascicle, beginning with "This transformative [consciousness] is only threefold," etc. Now, this single verse provides a detailed exposition.
That [consciousness] arises based on what is transformed by consciousness.
Here, the preceding section is concluded in order to link it to the subsequent section and initiate the discourse;
this marks the conclusion of the preceding part.
Treatise:
How should one understand [the progression] up to "there is only consciousness"?
Commentary:
This follows the preceding question.
From here below, the first two lines of the opening verse of the first fascicle are restated: "Due to the provisional designation of self and dharmas, various modes of transformation occur.
To the question of what those transformations depend upon—namely, that which is transformed by internal consciousness—it is said that these transforming [consciousnesses] are only three.
The preceding section has already separately explained the three transformations of consciousness.
Now, we shall explain how the provisional designations of self and phenomena are established based on the objects transformed by consciousness.
How is it that, based on the transformations of consciousness, the self and phenomena are provisionally established as having no separate, real existence?
Is it because all phenomena, which arise through the transformation of consciousness, are "consciousness-only" that this question is asked?
It is precisely to clarify the principle that all consciousnesses transform [into objects] that it is established as "consciousness-only.
This is the intent of the question.
He then cites the initial verse to introduce this inquiry.
The treatise states in verse: "Because [all things] reach [to that], all are representation-only (*vijñapti-mātra*)."
The commentary states:
The first half explains *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only),
while the second half concludes the discussion on *vijñapti-mātra*.
The prose commentary explains this itself;
I shall not trouble you by reproducing it here.
The treatise says:
Regarding the establishment of the term "transformation" (*pariṇāma*),
the commentary states:
the prose section consists of two parts.
First, the direct explanation of the verse;
second, the extensive analysis through questions and answers.
Regarding the direct explanation of the verse:
The first two sections provide the detailed explanation,
while the final section provides the summary.
Regarding the phrase "these various consciousnesses," this explains the first three characters of the opening line of the verse.
This refers to the three transforming consciousnesses, beginning with the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), together with their associated mental factors (*caitta*).
By saying "the king and his ministers," it mentions both the primary and the secondary. As An-hui (Sthiramati) explains:
What is meant by "transformation"?
It refers to the fact that the very substance of these three consciousnesses undergoes transformation, appearing as the two parts of the seeing and the seen.
This self-substance part of consciousness is what is called "transformation."
"Transformation" (pariṇāma) means the sense of manifestation;
that is, the self-substance of consciousness manifests as appearing like two aspects,
yet in reality it is not two aspects.
In fact, because these two characteristics are precisely what is grasped,
they exist as the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva) appearing upon the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva);
in ultimate reality, however, they do not exist at all.
Alternatively, "transformation" (pariṇāma) means "change" (anyathātva).

This refers to the single substance of consciousness transforming into the two functional divisions of the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) and the object-image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*). Master Dharmapāla explains as follows:
Furthermore, "transformation" (pariṇāma) means the sense of changing or shifting.
That is to say, the single substance of consciousness transforms and arises as two aspects, becoming distinct from its own essence;
thus, there appears the function of the grasper.
Characteristics such as having substantiality and resistance arise because consciousness, by its very nature,
evolves into a grasper and possesses resistance.
Alternatively, "transformation" (pariṇāma) has the meaning of manifestation,
as explained in the first fascicle; here,
however, it refers to the capacity of the self-substance (svabhāva) itself to undergo transformation.
This concludes the explanation of the first line of the verse. According to the treatise:
"The transformed seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) reaches the perceived object (grāhya)."
The commentary states:
Dharmapāla says that within the aforementioned transformations, the transformed seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) is termed "discrimination" (*vikalpa*).
This is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*),
because it grasps the dependent aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of its own transformations; thus,
it gives rise to various conceptual constructions of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
This is the function transformed from the essence of consciousness; because it is capable of conceptual discrimination, it is called "discrimination.

The aspect of the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) transformed from the essence of that consciousness—which resembles the aspect of the grasped (grāhya-bhāga)—is called the "object of discrimination" (vikalpya).
This is because it is the perceived characteristic (*nimitta*) grasped by the previously mentioned discerning seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*);
it does not mean that the self-substance of consciousness (*vijñāna-svabhāva*) can itself take an object and thus be called "discernment.
Rather, that which gives rise to discerning vision is the function of consciousness.
"Because both the image (*nimitta*) and the vision (*darśana*) arise based upon self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*). An-hui states:
"The transformed vision-portion and image-portion are both imputed as being grasped objects (*parikalpita*).
The vision resembles the grasper (*grāhaka*)."
The object of apprehension is similar to the seeing;
in reality, there are not two parts.
The second phrase has been explained.
Treatise:
By means of this correct principle, one reaches the state of being free from the two characteristics.
Commentary says:
He then employs the logic of the preceding two lines to explain the latter two lines of the verse.
Dharmapāla states:
"Therefore, those [entities] they postulate—real selves and dharmas external to the mind—"
The two parts—the dependent and the imagined—which are transformations of consciousness, are both definitely non-existent.
This does not mean that the transformation of consciousness is a real self or phenomena;
rather, it is because they appear as a self and phenomena.
Externally, the self and dharmas do not exist apart from consciousness.

This is because, apart from the substance of consciousness, there are no separate entities outside the apprehending aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) and the apprehended aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) that are transformed [by it].
This is true for all sentient beings; what is transformed by each is likewise so.
Based on these two divisions, the designations of "self" and "dharmas" are established;

for those two have no basis apart from these [divisions]. Question: What reason is there for not admitting that there exists a distinct, substantial entity separate from the transformation of the grasper and the grasped?
Answer: It is not the case that there exists a single, real, functional entity.
Because one is free from both the subject that discriminates and the object that is discriminated, there is no external self or phenomena; consciousness must necessarily exist.
Thus says An-hui (Sthiramati).
In reality, both the self and dharmas—which are apart from the two divisions transformed by consciousness—are non-existent.
This is because, apart from the imagined grasping at the duality of subject and object, they do not exist;
thus, based on this general non-existence, one establishes their specific non-existence.
That which is transformed by consciousness is collectively the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva).
Since no real entity exists apart from these two aspects,
all things are merely consciousness (vijñapti-mātra).
The explanation of the third phrase is concluded.
The treatise states: Therefore, all arrivals (*prāpti*) are not separate from consciousness.
The commentary states:
This explains the fourth line of the verse.
If conditioned and unconditioned phenomena were to arise from distinct seeds based on the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva), [then...]
Either eternally abiding real dharmas,
non-associated provisional dharmas,
or provisional dharmas such as jars.
All things are not separate from consciousness;
they are transformations of conditioned consciousness and the essence of unconditioned consciousness.
None of these exist outside of consciousness;
thus, it is said that names do not depart from consciousness.
This does not mean that the substance of all things is a single consciousness, which is what is meant by "consciousness-only" (vijñaptimātra).
Treatise:
The word "only" (kevalam/eva) is used to exclude [the possibility that it] reaches the mental factors and so forth.
Commentary: [As stated above.]
The term "consciousness-only" (vijñaptimātra) is so named because it excludes a real self or dharmas external to the transforming consciousnesses;
it does not exclude mental factors (caitta), nor the seeing and image aspects (darśana- and nimitta-bhāga), nor matter (rūpa), true suchness (tathatā), and so forth.
Therefore, because it is not separate from consciousness, it is called "consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*).
This concludes Dharmapāla’s explanation of the fourth line,
which also serves as a response to external objections.
Sthiramati explains the conventional and the real according to their respective contexts;
this refers to the first fascicle’s explanation of *pariṇāma* as "transformation.
This represents the doctrine of the two masters: the first being Master Dharmapāla and others, and the second being Master Sthiramati.
In the aspect of transformative penetration,
one perceives that there is still both existence and non-existence,
as explained in the first fascicle.
Based on the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) that has been transformed, the actual grasper is excluded;
based on the image-part (nimitta-bhāga) that has been transformed, the actual grasped is excluded.
Accordingly, both forms of grasping (dvaya-graha) are absent.
Regarding the preceding passage, An-hui (Sthiramati) states that the others are not [the Buddha's words],
whereas Dharmapāla maintains that they all apply universally,
or alternatively, that they are all with outflows (*sāsrava*).
This is because it explains conceptual differentiation (*vikalpa*). The treatise states:
"Alternatively, 'transformation' refers to the manifestation of the appearance of external objects."
The commentary states:
The following is the second explanation by Nanda and others;
the first [part] refers to the term "all consciousnesses."
This is explained by the same master as before;
therefore, it is not recounted again.
As for the term "transformation" (pariṇāma):

That is to say, the internal seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*) consciousnesses of the aforementioned three transformative [consciousnesses] are able to manifest the other-dependent image-division (*nimitta-bhāga*) as if it were an external object;
there is only the internal consciousness consisting of the seeing and image divisions.
There is no external object that undergoes transformation;
external objects generally consist of both the grasper and the grasped.
This is based on the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and other treatises, which explain that there are only these two meanings.
This does not state the position of the master who asserts the self-cognizing portion (*svasaṃvittibhāga*);
it differs from the former master’s view,
namely that [the mind] is the universal grasper (*parikalpaka*).
As well as the phenomena that are the objects of universal conceptualization (parikalpita),
both the grasper (grāhaka) and the grasped (grāhya) are merely false attachments to the appearance-portion (nimitta-bhāga) transformed by the mind as being separate entities.
Even if one maintains that the aspect of seeing is either the self or a phenomenon,
it is nonetheless not non-objective, because it is also grasped upon the transformations of the mind. Therefore, it is not the case that it is not an object-condition (*ālambana*).
Because these various consciousnesses possess the capacity to manifest as external objects, they are termed "transformation" (*pariṇāma*).
This concludes the explanation of the first phrase of the treatise.
"This is that which can transform the mind and mental factors.
Commentary:
This is the designation for the fault of false discrimination (*abhūtaparikalpa*).
Because the *Madhyāntavibhāga* and other treatises explain that the transforming consciousnesses have false discrimination as their intrinsic nature,
these are precisely the mind and mental factors of the three realms.
The commentary states: By means of the transformative expression in the first line of the verse,
one immediately [perceives] the essence of discrimination in the second line.
"This refers to the nature of the real self and dharmas as objects of grasping.
Commentary: Those persons and dharmas external to the mind are called the "discriminated."

Having thus cited the dependent nature as the "discriminating transformation" and concluded that the "imagined nature" is what is termed the "object of discrimination," the imagined nature is thereby established.
This explains the second line of the treatise:
"Because this conceptual differentiation has already been extensively refuted."
The commentary states:
Because the discriminating mind manifests as the appearance of real selves and dharmas external to the mind,
it is precisely by means of this discriminating mind [that such appearances arise].
Because they manifest as the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) in the form of the characteristics of the provisional self and dharmas,
those truly existent selves and dharmas— which are the objects of conceptualization and grasping by the parikalpita-svabhāva external to that mind—
are definitively non-existent.
That which is referred to in the verse as "the object of conceptualization" is the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*),
because it is that which is conceptually constructed by the mind of discrimination.
In substance, it does not exist at all. Why is this so?
Because in the first and second volumes previously cited, it has already been extensively refuted through both reasoning and scripture.
Because the transforming consciousness manifests as the appearance of an object,
there is no referent for the grasped external objects of the mind.
This concludes the explanation of the third phrase.
Treatise:
Therefore, all [these] reach the ultimate and are established as such. Commentary:
[As stated above.]
Conditioned and unconditioned phenomena, as well as real and provisional dharmas, all exist as nothing but consciousness.
Because it can transform through false discrimination,
the twenty schools and others teach that its essence is not non-existent.
Because it is universally established. Such being the case,
[the same applies to] true suchness (*tathatā*),
mental factors (*caitta*), and so forth.
It is not that the mind can transform what is discriminated,
nor is it that there are phenomena discriminated outside the mind;
this constitutes existence and non-existence.
Treatise:
Since "only" does not exclude that which reaches [the object], it also possesses substantial existence (*dravyasat*).
Commentary: [As stated above.]
The word "only" does not exclude phenomena that are not separate from consciousness;
such as true thusness (tathatā) and mental factors (caitta), etc.
Furthermore, because they do not exist apart from consciousness, their substance exists in all cases.
Here, however, we merely negate that which is conceptually constructed as existing apart from consciousness;
we do not negate the existence of such things as true thusness (tathatā), which do not exist apart from consciousness.
This should be understood according to the principle;
thus the explanation of the fourth phrase is concluded.
Since this [consciousness] possesses the evolving discerning consciousness (*vikalpa-vijñāna*), it is as follows.
Furthermore, the objects transformed and the dependent characteristics—
the mind that performs the discrimination and external real dharmas and so forth— definitively do not exist at all; therefore,
there is only consciousness.
Suchness, the mental factors, and so forth are all not separate from consciousness,
and they are also substantially existent.
This text establishes the name "discrimination" because it refers only to the state of being with outflows (*sāsrava*).
The treatise states:
"By means of this, one becomes detached and reaches the realization of the Middle Way."
The commentary states:
This is a summary.
By means of these two passages and the principles of the three masters, one remains far removed from the two extremes.
Because there are no phenomena external to the mind, the extreme of reification is eliminated;
because there is the illusory mind and so forth, the extreme of nihilism is avoided.
Because one avoids the extreme of nihilism...
This excludes the assertions of those such as Bhāviveka, who negate [external objects] like flowers in the sky,
because it avoids the extreme of superimposition;
it also excludes the attachments of the various Hīnayāna schools that maintain the existence of phenomena apart from the mind.
The meaning of Consciousness-Only (Vijñaptimātra) is established as being in accord with the Middle Way,
because it is free from biased attachments.
What is called the "Middle Way" is correct cognition (samyagjñāna).
The principle of accordant correct wisdom is called "conforming to the Middle Way.
The three masters mentioned above have already explained the transformation of consciousness and completed their commentary on the verse.
Hereafter follows the second section, consisting of nine questions and answers.
There are ten points in total.
The first concerns the difficulty regarding the causes of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*).
Within this initial question-and-answer section, there are five parts.
First, the question;
second, the answer;
third, the inquiry.
Four explanations;
five conclusions.
Treatise.
By what scriptural authority and reasoning is the doctrine of *vijñaptimātra* established?
The commentary states:
First, the external opponent asks.
Treatise:
Has this not already been explained? Commentary: It has.
The author of this treatise answers:
that is to say, from the first fascicle to the second fascicle,
he initially establishes it as the underlying principle.
Furthermore, in the second fascicle, two verses from the *Ghanavyūha-sūtra* have already been cited as proof;
therefore, it is said that they have "already been explained. Thus says the treatise.
Although it has been explained, the principle of this teaching has not yet been fully established.
The commentary states: A third opponent asks:
Although this has already been briefly explained above, it remains incomplete.
Although the doctrine of the self (*ātman*) was refuted previously,
the establishment of our own position does not follow merely by virtue of refuting the opponent's position.
One should further state with certainty the teachings and reasoning that establish this Vijñaptimātra.
"Certainty" means ultimate reality.
This is the treatise.
As stated in the Sūtra, up to the point where it says "manifested by consciousness-only.
The commentary states:
This is the explanation of the four masters.
The first part answers regarding the teaching;
the latter reveals the principle.
Within the section on the teaching, six textual passages are initially enumerated.

The subsequent general reference, "the three realms are mind-only," is the text from the sixth stage (*ṣaṣṭhī bhūmiḥ*) of the eighth fascicle of the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, as taught in the *Avataṃsaka*.
Vasubandhu’s *Triṃśikā-bhāṣya* (Chapter 4) provides no explanation for this.
The fourth chapter of *Munimatālaṃkāra* provides an extensive explanation of the names and essential nature (*svabhāva*) of the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*.
Regarding the statement "mind-only" (*cittamātra*),
"mind" (*citta*) and "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) are one and the same.
The word "only" (kevala) serves to exclude the object of apprehension;
because that [object] does not exist, the subject of apprehension also does not exist.
This does not, however, preclude the existence of mental factors (caitta).
Because they are inseparable.
As it is said: "If there were no mental factors, the mind would never have arisen.
This refers to the statement that "the three realms are mind-only."
This demonstrates that the three realms are consciousness-only;
it shows that one falls into the three realms through association with the fetters of craving, such as desire,
and that one belongs to the three realms by virtue of the fetters of greed and so forth.
This statement of "consciousness-only" (vijñapti-mātra) does not negate objects of cognition that are falsely imagined (parikalpita),
nor does it exclude the object of cognition that is suchness (tathatā), nor the object of cognition that is the dependent nature (paratantra).
This refers to that which is the object of the two types of wisdom— the fundamental and the subsequently attained— subsumed under the Truth of the Path;
for it is not grasped by craving and is not something to be remedied.
Because it is not delusory,
it is not subsumed within the three realms;
furthermore, because it is not separate from consciousness, this need not be stated.
It is not that there are no untainted (*anāsrava*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharmas. If that were so, one could say that the two realms of desire and form are "mind-only";
thus, it would be stated that these two realms are mind-only.
Why, then, does it further state that the formless realm is "mind-only"?
This is because followers of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) and others mostly reckon those realms to be mere consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*);
thus, [the statement] would be proving what is already established for them. This is not the case.
Not only is form absent,
but there is also no grasping mind such as craving; therefore,
there is likewise no other object of cognition, such as empty space, which is apprehended by consciousness.
Furthermore, the Sautrāntikas maintain that formless minds and so forth are formless and lack substantiality,
serving as the basis for the manifestation of unreal objects of perception.
Fearing that they might hold these to be non-mind, it is said that "the three realms are mind-only."
This is precisely the meaning of the doctrine of Mind-Only (*cittamātra*); it is thus.
Furthermore, regarding the two previous masters, there are two alternative interpretations.
Here, because it refers to the deluded mind that gives rise to grasping, it speaks only of the "three realms" (*tridhātu*).

Otherwise, the untainted (*anāsrava*) would not be mere consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*). Furthermore, the statement that "the object of cognition is what is manifested by mere consciousness" is a passage from the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*;
the seventy-sixth [chapter] explains it with this same intent.
Regarding what you claim to be an external object of cognition,
I say that it is merely an unreal external phenomenon appearing upon internal consciousness.
Vasubandhu states:
This means that the objects of consciousness are merely manifestations of consciousness itself, without any separate objective referents.
To state "consciousness" once again is to demonstrate that what is manifested by the "self" (the subject) is definitively the domain of consciousness;
that which is manifested as "mere consciousness" has no separate ontological substance.
乃至佛告慈氏：無有少法能取少法，無作用故。 Even unto the Buddha’s address to Maitreya:
"There is not even the slightest dharma that can grasp another slight dharma,
because there is no functional activity."
However, when a phenomenon arises, the power of dependent origination is such that two reflections arise within a single entity; these,
in relation to one another, are neither identical nor separate.
All minds and mental factors arise by the power of conditions through their own inherent nature (*dharmatā*),
just as a reflection arises dependent upon a physical object and so forth;
herein, these are mentioned briefly.
Treatise:
It is further stated that all phenomena do not exist apart from the mind.
Commentary: [As follows:]
The text of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* appears in various places throughout its preceding and succeeding sections;
it would be impossible to point them all out exhaustively.
Treatise:
It is further stated that sentient beings follow the defilement or purity of their minds.
Commentary: [As follows].
Now, regarding the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*,
the old translation titled *Weimojie jing* states:
"Because the mind is pure, sentient beings are pure."
Because the mind is defiled, sentient beings are defiled.
As previously established in the fourth fascicle, the eighth [verse] has already been cited as proof.
It does not state that there is defilement or purity because of following after form and so forth; therefore, it is "mind-only."
Treatise:
Furthermore, it is said that one achieves the realization that there is only consciousness and no external objects.
Commentary: [As follows].
The text has three parts:
first, a general enumeration;
second, a detailed exposition.
This is then concluded;
this is the first [stage].
If one accomplishes the four wisdoms, one can enter Consciousness-Only and realize the ten stages (*bhūmi*) in the present.
Those who enter [the path] through realization are those prior to the stages (bhūmi).
Alternatively, they enter the ten stages in accordance with the meaning of the sūtras.
That which explains the locus of the four wisdoms is called the *Catuḥjñāna-sūtra*.
However, this is the Abhidharma-sūtra;
the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* merely states, "As the Blessed One has said," without specifying the location of the sūtra.
Treatise:
How is it that the cognition of the characteristics of contradictory perceptions is established?
The commentary states:
The following section specifically elucidates the four wisdoms.
As Asvabhāva states:
"They are called 'contradictory' because they are mutually opposed."
Contradiction is the object itself,
because each has its own distinct nature.
That which possesses contradiction is called "the contradictory."
Alternatively, "contradictory" refers to the fact that both the person and the object are distinct;
that which is contradictory is called a "contradictory cognition."
The cause for the arising of this consciousness is termed the "objective aspect" (*nimitta*).
The wisdom of a bodhisattva realizes that this aspect is solely the internal mind;
therefore, all phenomena are likewise merely transformations of the mind.
The pus-rivers of the hungry ghosts,
the dwelling-roads of the fish,
and the ground adorned with celestial jewels.
The person is like clear, cool water;
the concentration on emptiness is simply emptiness.
These are not two distinct, substantial entities that are mutually contradictory.
Although this [object] does not exist as a thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), nevertheless, the categories of karma transform accordingly so that each appears differently.
As it was said in older translations: "A single object should correspond to the four minds."
Now, regarding the object (*viṣaya*):
since it is not necessarily one,
it should be said to be "in one place" (*ekadeśa*).
The treatise states: "By understanding that there is no object of perception, one realizes that there is only consciousness;
this same principle applies to all other cases as well."
The commentary states:
Regarding the second point, the refutation of [the Sarvāstivāda] views on the past and future, there is no commonality with the Sautrāntika position;
as has already been refuted above, this is the same as the critique of the Sarvāstivāda.
Therefore, it is established as being without an object. "The wisdom of the wise" refers to the wisdom of the bodhisattvas.
"Consciousness without an object" means consciousness that lacks an object;
this refers to all consciousnesses that take the past or the future as their objects.
This is mind-only.
Because Bodhisattvas take this consciousness as their object and can give rise [to cognition] without an external realm, it is called "wisdom."
The old [tradition] says that because conditions are non-existent, apprehension cannot arise;
the present [tradition] says that in the Mahāyāna, the *parikalpita* (imagined) aspect must necessarily exist.
One should say, however, that the object is not real.
The treatise states: "One should contemplate that what is realized through direct knowledge is that there is only consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*).
This is the third [point]: one should possess non-erroneous wisdom and thereby attain liberation."
The commentary states:
If all ordinary beings had already attained the real object,
it would be because that object is not false.
In that case, all ordinary beings would spontaneously attain liberation without effort;
since liberation is not thus achieved, there is only consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*).
Formerly it was said that the "difficult dust" (dusty objects) are substantially existent;
now it is said that the wisdom realizing [emptiness] is not established [as such],
for one realizes through direct knowledge that there is only consciousness.
The following passage discusses how the objects [of meditation] follow the transformation of the three types of wisdom.
The treatise asks:
"How can the objects of the four [applications of mindfulness] be transformed according to the transformation of the three knowledges?"
The commentary states:
First, "attaining mastery over the mind" means that the mind has become disciplined and compliant, such that it is capable of performing its functions.
If one is superior, it is only from the eighth bhūmi onwards that one can spontaneously and truly transform the great earth and so forth into gold and jewels for the use of sentient beings.
The objective sphere transforms according to wisdom, whereby all that is desired is accomplished.
Alternatively, although the objective sphere may also be accomplished through contemplation based on mental resolve (*adhimukti-manasikāra*),
here we take the transformation of the essential nature (*svabhāva-parāvṛtti*) and not this [latter case].
The previous interpretation is correct.
Furthermore, with respect to attaining the ten masteries (*vaśitā*),
all ten stages (*bhūmi*) attain them.
Based on this principle, mastery over meditative concentration (*samādhi-vaśitā*) is attained;
it may be transformed already in the first stage (*bhūmi*), or mastery over meditative concentration is attained in the third stage.
These are stated according to what is predominant in each case.
However, all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who are able to perform this act do so because their wisdom operates in accordance with the objects and circumstances.
Treatise.
Second, regarding "observing accordingly":
when wisdom transforms, does that wisdom follow the transformation of the mind?

and these respective perceived (nimitta) and seeing (darśana) parts transformed by them.
The three natures, the three realms, the nine stages, outflows, non-outflows, retribution, and non-retribution—
whichever of these manifest individually and are capable of acting as perfumers (vāsanā) are precisely what is meant.
However, among these seven consciousnesses and so forth,
with the exception of all wholesome dharmas belonging to the stage of Buddhahood,
the remainder pertain to the causal stage.
Furthermore, because all untainted (anāsrava) states, such as those of the two vehicles’ adepts (aśaikṣa),
are capable of perfuming,
among the tainted (sāsrava) states, only the extremely inferior indeterminate (avyākṛta) states are excluded.
This refers to the four types of neutral states (*avyākṛta*), excluding those born of maturation (*vipākaja*).

Within the category of those born of maturation, there are other neutral states not subsumed under the remaining three types, which are termed "neutral states born of maturation," such as the class of grasping at dharmas (*dharmagrāha*) and so forth.
All of these are capable of perfuming,
with the sole exception of that which is summoned by karma within the six consciousnesses;
for compared to other neutral states, it is extremely weak.
The eighth consciousness is also excluded;
for those things attracted solely by karma are not capable of perfuming.
Having thus excluded one from each category of the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), [the remaining factors constitute the perfumers].
All other contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) factors manifesting as views, mental concomitants (*saṃskāra*), and so forth,

infuse the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) to produce their own respective seeds, categorized by their own kind, realm (*dhātu*), stage (*bhūmi*), and whether they are contaminated or uncontaminated.
This manifestation serves as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) solely in relation to those seeds.
Among these, the wholesome qualities of the Buddha-fruit and the extremely inferior indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) states do not perfume and thereby form seeds.
All of this is as explained in the second fascicle, within the section on the four meanings of the capable and the perfumable.
[This is because] in the eighth category of mind, there is nothing that can be perfumed.
The commentary states:
From this point downward, there is a concise summary.
This summary consists of three parts.
This is the first [point].
Within the aforementioned "perfuming agents" (bhāvakas),
for what reason is there no eighth mental complex (citta-varga)?

The term "mental category" (citta-varga) refers generally to the seeing, the concomitants, and the dharmas associated with them. Answer: This is because the eighth mental category has nothing further to be perfumed; it is itself that which is perfumed.
The other seven are all capable of perfuming.
If that were so, then the eight mental factors accompanying the mind should also be capable of perfuming, because they are perfumed by the primary mind (citta).
[Treatise:]
"Because it is not the case that [the object] alone can perfuse, setting aside its basis.
The commentary states:
"This does not exclude the mind which serves as the basis."

And because mental factors alone are capable of perfuming. Question: If the mind-king (*cittarāja*), when distinguished from mental factors, is still uniquely the object of perfuming (*bhāvyamāna*), what prevents mental factors—when distinguished from the mind-king—from being uniquely capable of perfuming? Answer: The mind-king possesses sovereignty (*vaśitva*).
That which is autonomous alone is capable of perfuming;
mental factors lack autonomy and thus cannot perfume alone.
Treatise:
Because the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*) is spherical, it does not perfume [the mind] to form seeds.
Commentary says:
Furthermore, regarding the interpretation that the eighth consciousness within the causal state and the maturation-consciousness (*vipāka-citta*) among the six consciousnesses are both non-perfuming:
because they are extremely subtle, they are incapable of perfuming.
Because the power of dharmas born of maturation (*vipāka*) is extremely weak and they arise merely through spontaneity,
that which is capable of perfuming must necessarily not be a dharma lacking power; therefore,
because atoms (*paramāṇu*) are [such] within the causal state, they are not capable of perfuming.
The seventh manas of those without intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva) also possesses power,
as has been explained previously.
This refers to the eighth [consciousness] at the stage of Buddhahood.
Because it is perfectly complete, it does not form seeds through perfuming.
Since the wholesome dharmas of the Buddha-body neither increase nor decrease,
it is held that if they were further perfumed, they would no longer be perfect.
Because it gradually increases,
by this principle,
it is the eighth [stage] within the causal state.
Furthermore, those mental factors (*caitta*) are all incapable of perfuming; therefore,
the preceding treatise states that there are only seven [capable of perfuming].
Treatise:
Because manifest activities of the same category arise from their own seeds. Commentary:
[As stated above].
Second, the brief summary: Question—Why is it that when similar [dharmas] manifest, the preceding is like the "similar cause" (*sabhāga-hetu*) of the Hīnayāna?
Is this not a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*)? Answer—Because within the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*), each arises from its own respective seed.
Because there are causes and conditions capable of directly producing its own substance;
the preceding manifestation is not a causal condition for the subsequent one,
and this is likewise true for all external things such as barley and the like.
Question: Why is it that all seeds— whether simultaneous or non-simultaneous—
are of a different category from the manifest [dharmas],
and why are seeds themselves of a different category from one another?
Manifest activity in relation to another manifest activity of a different category,
and manifest activity in relation to its seeds of a different category,
are in neither case a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
Treatise:
Because all things of different categories do not arise from immediate production. Commentary:
[As stated above].
The third is the concise [explanation],
as stated herein: viewed in relation to one another,
they are likewise not causal conditions (*pratyaya*).

Since it has already been stated that heterogeneous classes [of dharmas] cannot directly produce either simultaneous or asynchronous results of a heterogeneous class, [this is addressed in] the treatise.
Some say this refers to the gate of reaching a different category or the gate of following along.
The commentary states:
from here below, there are two ways to understand the resolution of the objections.
As stated in the fourth [chapter] of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*:
"Those of different categories and those of the same category act as mutual causes and conditions for their manifestation.
Regarding this, within the section on causes and conditions in that *Abhidharma* treatise:
It is taught that the six causes constitute the conditioned cause (*hetu-pratyaya*). This refers specifically to the present [cause] in relation to the present [result].
Even if there are other instances where this is taught elsewhere, [the principle remains the same].
These are all conventionally designated as causes and conditions,
because they are in reality predominating conditions (*adhipatipratyaya*) and so forth.
Alternatively, this is according to the perspective of the "conforming gate" (*anuvartana-mukha*).
The *Sarvāstivāda* school asserts that the five causes, such as the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), constitute the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*);
however, the eighteenth fascicle of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* refutes those five causes, demonstrating that they do not constitute the causal condition.
One should explain it as follows.
The treatise states that there are those who assert that only the seed reaching [the fruit] constitutes the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
The commentary states: Furthermore,
the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, in its third, fifth, fifty-first, thirty-eighth, and other chapters, as well as the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, in its eighteenth chapter and others,
all exclusively state that the seed alone is the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
This is stated to highlight its preeminence and is not an exhaustive description of its nature.
How is its preeminence highlighted?
It is because it is constant and continuous.
The "superior manifestation" is like a grain producing a sprout,
because the characteristic is manifested in the active process; thus,
it is now said that it manifests the superior.
Based on the fifty-first [chapter] of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*,
which cite the *Abhidharma-sūtra* and other sources,
it is taught that the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) and the ālayavijñāna serve as mutual causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).
Since it is not their own seeds,
one cannot say that the evolving consciousnesses (pravṛttivijñāna) and the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) serve as mutual causes and conditions for one another; thus,
we know that the six and the seventh [consciousnesses] arise in the present.
It serves as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) for the seed fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*),
because it functions in the sense that the manifest state (*pravṛtti*) perfumes and forms seeds;
thus, by means of the brief, the extensive is revealed.

Therefore, one should know that all contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) seeds and manifest activities (*samudācāra*) mentioned above constitute the substance of the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
Treatise:
Second, the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) brings about their certain arising.
The commentary states:
Within this, there are three parts;
first, the definition of its essence.
Next is the brief summary;
the subsequent section will explain the characteristics.
This is the first [part]. Regarding "the eight manifest consciousnesses and their mental factors":
The substance of the objective condition consists solely of the perceived object and self-cognition; this is the general designation for the manifesting consciousness (*nirbhāsa-vijñāna*).

This excludes matter (*rūpa*), the dissociated factors (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), seeds (*bīja*), and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), as these do not possess the nature of being this objective condition.
Because many similar types of matter (rūpa) that are non-associated (viprayukta) evolve simultaneously with their seeds,
it is stated in the *Triṃśikā* [verse 38] that the immediately preceding condition (samanantarapratyaya) is spoken of only in relation to all minds (citta) and mental factors (caitta).
Because it is embraced by the guidance provided in previous lives:
"opening" (kai) has the sense of avoiding [obstacles] and providing space for what follows.
"Guiding" (nāyaka) has the meaning of "attracting.
That is to say, the preceding dharma avoids its own position and attracts the subsequent one, causing it to arise.
Only when there is a causal dharma do these two [functions] become complete.
Since it is known from the Bodhisattva-bhūmi that there are statements providing guidance,
[it is clear that] although the individual entities of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and the homogeneous group (*nikāyasabhāga*) are each single, they do not arise simultaneously.
First, it is provisional;
second, it lacks the function of being an object-condition.
If it were a phenomenon that serves as an object of cognition or provides guidance, [it would possess these functions].
Furthermore, it is not the case that this condition exists only for those things that are provisional.
However, the meaning of "provisional" alone does not exclude the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and so forth,
because even though non-negligence (*apramāda*) and other such factors are provisional, they also possess this condition.

The life-faculty (jīvitendriya) possesses the sense of being an equal-and-immediate condition (samanantara-pratyaya), but it lacks the sense of being an object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) because it does not have the sense of opening the way [for the subsequent moment]. Regarding the phrase "the preceding aggregate for the subsequent":
this excludes those that are simultaneous or subsequent from being the object-condition for what precedes them.
"Because it is not an opening and guiding [condition]" means that its own kind [of consciousness] is indicated as being the condition, and not another consciousness.
"Immediately preceding" indicates that although the immediately preceding [moment] serves as the condition for the subsequent one, [it does so as an object-condition].
There is no interval of intermediate existence;
it must be immediate,
even if there has been a cessation for as long as a hundred years.
It is also for this reason that the fifth fascicle of the Abhidharma states: "If it were not so,
the mind would enter the mindless meditative absorption."
One would expect that the mind emerging from meditative absorption should not be its object-condition;
therefore, it is known that, by analogy, the meaning of being an object-condition applies to consciousness of its own kind.
Otherwise, [this would not hold].
The mind emerging from meditative absorption is induced by the seventh and eighth consciousnesses;
how could these not be the conditions that open and guide it?
This reveals the single mind that has just ceased.
The final mind and its mental concomitants serve as the object-condition for all preceding minds and their mental concomitants;
conversely, all preceding minds and their mental concomitants serve as the object-condition for the single final mind.
Because the mind is equal and provides guidance, it is called "equal guidance" (*samanvāhāra*).
This refers to that which equally pertains to both preceding and succeeding moments, encompassing both cause and effect;
it thus distinguishes [the true] meaning of the *śramaṇa* from merely similar phenomena.
Because each of those individual mental factors (citta-samprayukta-dharma) serves as a condition for itself, but not for others;
furthermore, the term "and so forth" [indicates this].
This reveals that within the collection of mind and mental factors, there is only one mind and only one mental factor at a time; likewise for subsequent moments.
Therefore, because a single dharma is not manifold, it is established as being equal [to others].
It is not as in the case of matter (*rūpa*), where multiple categories of non-associated [formations] arise within a single aggregate;
for those are not equal.
Furthermore, although the eight consciousnesses within a single body are called "multiple categories," [they do not arise simultaneously].
However, while the essence (*tattva*) and function (*vṛtti*) are distinct, names such as "equality" and so forth [apply to them];
in the case of phenomena such as form (*rūpa*), there is no distinction between essence and function,
and because many types arise simultaneously, they are not equal.
Examples such as grass and fire should be understood accordingly.
"Opening and guiding" clarifies the meaning of the condition (*pratyaya*); "causing that [result] to definitely arise" clarifies the subsequent fruit (*phala*).
Even though a vast period of time has elapsed, such as eighty thousand kalpas,
the preceding visual consciousness still serves as a condition for the subsequent one,
because the later and later effects are certain to arise.
That is to say, the final moment of consciousness in the state of nirvana without remainder (anupadhiśeṣa) is excluded;
because it does not give rise to a subsequent fruit, it is not this condition.
Although it possesses the sense of "opening" [the way], it lacks the power of guidance.
That material phenomena (rūpadharma) are not equal [to consciousness] is established by the world;
that non-associated [conditioned factors] are merely nominal is the tenet of our own school (svasiddhānta);
and that unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta) lack the characteristics of priority and posteriority is admitted by both ourselves and others.
Now, it should be understood that seeds do not possess the characteristics of this [mutual] condition.
The treatise states:
"Many seeds of the same category do not serve as mutual conditions for one another."

This excludes the seeds [of the sense organs],
for the seeds of the visual consciousness have been evolving simultaneously with hundreds of thousands of similar types from beginningless time until the present.
Just as the dissociated (*viprayukta*) factors are not included among these conditions,
this analogy is cited to simultaneously demonstrate that they are not conditions,
because they lack the meaning of "equality" (*samatā*).
Because seeds and non-associated factors can coexist in multiple instances, it is not logical for them to function as conditions [for one another];
thus, the eight consciousnesses do not serve as mutual conditions for one another,
as they arise simultaneously in various categories.
If a single consciousness were to act as its own condition,
it could not be manifold simultaneously,
because it is unitary by nature.
If it is granted that the eight consciousnesses mutually serve as conditions for one another,
and that multiple types arising together can function as conditions,
then this must also apply to the category of seeds.
Because the eight manifest consciousnesses differ in both essence and function, they are not of the same category;
unlike seeds and so forth, which belong to a single class and number in the hundreds or thousands.

"Mind-associates [serve as] the equal-and-immediate condition for the mind.

this indicates that they are indeed mind-associates.
Although mental factors and the mind always arise together,
because they are associated (*samprayukta*), they are harmonized as if they were one;
they share the same object of cognition (*ālambana*).
Furthermore, they share the same basis,
arise at the same time,
and are subsumed within the same nature.

They cannot be separated so as to become distinct, for they do not differ from the eight consciousnesses in their modes of activity (*ākāra*), objects (*ālambana*), or bases (*āśraya*); thus, they do not serve as mutual conditions for one another.
The distinction made here is as explained previously in the fifth fascicle, in the section on the "basis of the opening of the path" (*mārga-āśraya*).
Treatise:
Because one has entered the state of nirvana without remainder, it is not the condition for this.
Commentary: [As stated above].
The final mind at the end is excluded because it is not [the path];
since the mind entering *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* is extremely feeble,
it lacks the functional capacity to open the way.
The application of mind in opening the path must possess power, for it is not feeble;
thus, it is because the causal power is weak [in the other case].
Furthermore, there would be no immediate fruit arising in accordance with that cause.
Therefore, that final mind is not included within this causal category.
As stated in the Eightieth [Treatise]:
"Prior to entering the mind of nirvana-without-remainder, one first enters the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) to extinguish the six evolving consciousnesses."
Subsequently, the remaining consciousnesses are extinguished.
There are cases where one enters the meditative attainment of cessation through the power of a vow and subsequently passes away;
this is because the untainted sixth consciousness has entered that meditative state.

An external opponent asks a proximate question.
How is it known that the final mind is not a condition?
The meaning of the remote question is:
how is it known that the preceding mental aggregate serves as a condition for the subsequent mental aggregate, rather than each individual [moment] serving as a condition for one another?

The Commentary says:
Furthermore, to answer the recent question:

as stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Great Treatise), fascicles 3 and 93, and the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (Exposition of the Noble Teachings), fascicle 18, this is identical to the present text. If this consciousness is immediately [preceded by]...
That is to say, when there is a condition, those [factors] such as consciousness necessarily arise.
This explains the existence of the fruit;
for the treatise states that they "necessarily arise."
Only when a fruit is certain to arise can it function as a condition;
furthermore, we do not maintain that the duration of time is fixed.

Since the fruit of entering the mind of nirupadhiśeṣa (nirvana without remainder) is not necessarily produced, it does not serve as this condition. This answers the previous question regarding distance.
Since it is stated that these [subsequent] consciousnesses arise immediately after [the preceding],
it clarifies that they take consciousness as their condition;
the fact that all consciousnesses arise determinately clarifies that the result extends to mental factors (caitta) as well.
Because the expression "and so forth" (ādi) is used regarding consciousness,
since it is already admitted that resultant dharmas can pertain to a single aggregate,
the conditions must likewise be so.
This is the analysis and determination of the nature of establishment and abandonment.

Regarding this:
Because there is no interruption until one reaches the state beyond outflows (*anāsrava*).

There is no case where the untainted (anāsrava) gives rise to the tainted (sāsrava).

Treatise:
From which realm is this subsequently induced to produce the untainted (anāsrava)?
Commentary states:
The opponent asks:
Since it is said that this eighth consciousness, being contaminated (*sāsrava*), gives rise to the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*),
in which realm does the contaminated arise prior to the production of the uncontaminated?
Treatise:
It is either from the Form Realm or from the Desire Realm.
The commentary states:
The author of this treatise answers:
from the two realms, subsequent existence arises as both contaminated and uncontaminated;
this refers collectively to two types of persons.
It is not [the case] in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), because there is no basis (*āśraya*) and because there is no benefit for others (*parārtha*).
Treatise.
This refers to the fact that all ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) attain enlightenment.
The commentary states:
"All ordinary beings."
As for those who attain Buddhahood through sudden enlightenment,
they certainly receive the benefit of successive retributions in the Form Realm (rūpadhātu),
because they are born in the abode of Mahesvara’s wisdom.
This is because there are no practitioners of the Two Vehicles in the Form Realm who turn their minds [toward the Mahāyāna].
As the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle eighty, states: "The birth-body retained within the death-and-rebirth of transformation belongs precisely to this continent."
Because there are no Buddhas or others to be converted there,
he resolves to remain in his body solely within the desire realm,
and will certainly be born in the Palace of Sovereignty (Vaśavartin).
Only ordinary beings [attain it] after the form realm;
those in training and others who turn their minds [toward the Mahāyāna] do so only within the levels of the desire realm and so forth.
According to the extent to which birth and death are exhausted,
one immediately undergoes transformation and birth;
subsequently, one proceeds to the Palace of Sovereignty to attain Buddhahood.
Because they do not go to be born there,
those ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) lack the death-and-rebirth of transformation (pariṇāmi-cyuti) within the bodies of the desire realm.
This is because the death-and-rebirth of transformation cannot involve dying and being reborn again in the palace of Maheśvara.
Upon reaching the eighth stage, the body must be reborn in the fourth dhyāna;

As for the "Palace of Maheśvara":
This means that above the Śuddhāvāsa heavens there exists a truly pure land;
it is there that the self-enjoyment body first arises through realization.

The old term was *Mahesvara*;
now it should be called *Maheśvara*, which is to say,
Maheśvara (the Great Lord).

the Reward Body (vipākakāya) of Bodhisattvas on the ten stages (daśabhūmi) proceeds there.
However, because their maturation belongs to the same level,

in reality, they undergo transformation.
While dwelling in the three lower realms,
one has not yet attained birth in the Pure Land;

for a Bodhisattva of the tenth stage, through the power of extreme cultivation,
is able to be born therein.

this is because those of the two vehicles who turn toward [the Mahāyāna] reach this point while still within the desire realm.

All those of the two vehicles, whether in training (śaikṣa) or beyond training (aśaikṣa), who resolve their minds in the desire realm,
will certainly produce the outflow-free (anāsrava) state subsequent to the desire realm.
Because they maintain their bodies through the power of their vows solely within the desire realm,
and because there are no such noble beings who have turned their minds [toward enlightenment] in the higher realms;
it is therefore said that only in the desire realm is there the initial generation of the mind of awakening.
Furthermore, the preservation of the body occurs only in the desire realm,
because there is no condition for the initial generation of the mind of enlightenment there;
nor is there the generation of the mind from a lower realm.
Having died, one is born in a higher realm while leaving behind the physical body;
thus, after the desire realm, the outflow-free state is induced.
However, at the time of attaining Buddhahood...
It is necessary to proceed to the Palace of Sovereignty (Īśvarabhavana) to attain Buddhahood,
as it is a supreme location; therefore,
one should know that this occurs after having undergone the transformation of the body (pariṇāmikakāya).
When one later travels to the Form Realm or various Pure Lands,
it should be understood that one is able to go there solely by means of the supernormal power of this very body.
It is not a case of further rebirth,
because the eightieth fascicle does not state that there is further rebirth through transformation (*pariṇāmi*).
Some say that the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* itself permits multiple births through transformation.
This contradicts this treatise;
I have examined the sūtra texts and found no explicit statement [to that effect].
This will be reconciled later, in the eighth fascicle, within the section on the two kinds of birth-and-death, as in other essential summaries.

adorns it in various ways, and places it in a pure location,

[and so on] as extensively explained above.

since it is accepted that those of the two vehicles who have attained the first or second fruits undergo birth by transformation (*pariṇāmika-janman*), even though they may initially resolve their minds [for enlightenment],

The first says that there are none.
One born in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) necessarily does not pass through a birth in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
An *anāgāmin* noble one who has attained the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*) knows that their karma of the desire realm is exhausted;
however, they may or may not have attained the fundamental meditative absorptions (*mauladhyāna*).
Because they have not yet attained supernormal powers, they are not mutually cognizant;
yet, being weary of the coarse body, they immediately and urgently draw forth the death-rebirth of transformation (*pariṇāmika-janma*).
Therefore, it is only in the upper realms that one undergoes the death-rebirth of transformation.
Because one who generates the resolve in the desire realm undergoes transformation (pariṇāma) within that very desire realm,
they are not the same as those in the first two fruits [of stream-entry and once-returning].
Their karmic actions of desire are not yet exhausted;
although they may know the extent of their karma,
there are also those who do not know it.
Drawn by the power of karma,
some undergo this cycle of birth and death at the very moment they resolve their minds [for awakening],
while others do not undergo it until as late as their seventh birth, and so forth.
One who has not yet returned to the state of non-retrogression will necessarily be reborn immediately,
because the power of karma is exhausted and the power of the Path is fulfilled.
Because their revulsion is profound,
they are unwilling to undergo even one more birth in the higher realms, let alone many.
Second, since there is no scriptural prohibition against it,
just as those who will be reborn seven times may resolve to prolong their lives at different times,
the same applies to non-returners (anāgāmin).
When one generates the mind directed toward the upper realms while remaining in the body of the desire realm,
the karmic force of that desire-realm body is exhausted; furthermore,
one has not yet attained the "limitless concentration" (prāntakoṭika-samādhi) that could sustain the remaining karma.
Because one desires to obtain a superior body as a basis for transformation,
according to this principle,
there may be those from higher realms who, having taken birth in only a single location, undergo rebirth there once more.
They are then about to undergo transformation;
there may be two stages or three stages,
or one ground, two grounds, three grounds, and even up to four grounds.
They reach the Heaven of Vast Results (Bṛhatphala) to receive a transformation body (nirmāṇakāya),
proceeding to the Sovereign Lord (Īśvara) to receive the rank of Buddhahood;
or some, even going as far as receiving only one more birth in the fourth dhyāna, undergo transformation.
Since there exists determinate karma (*niyata-karma*), there is no contradiction with reason. From this discussion, another point arises:
above the Śuddhāvāsa [Heavens], there is a realm of actual retribution (*vipāka-bhūmi*) which is the abode of those in the tenth stage (*daśamī-bhūmi*).
Is it not the case that this belongs to the three realms?

Because it is the place where the Dharma is preached for the Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage,
it is subsumed under the Heaven of Ultimate Purity (Akaniṣṭha).
This is because even the Pure Abodes (Śuddhāvāsa), being of supreme excellence, do not know of it nor reach it.

Question: Why is it that the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), like the mind preceding entry into the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), also possesses the untainted (*anāsrava*), yet is not subsumed under these three faculties?

Treatise: Although the Peak of Existence possesses [the faculties], it does not possess the latter three faculties. Commentary: *The term "possesses" (yǒu) refers to the presence of the faculties within that realm.* The "latter three faculties" refer to the faculty of suffering, the faculty of mental pleasure, and the faculty of equanimity. Although the Peak of Existence possesses the faculty of equanimity, it lacks the faculty of suffering because it is free from physical pain; it lacks the faculty of mental pleasure because it is free from the joy associated with the first dhyāna; and it lacks the faculty of faith and so forth because they are absent in the state of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*). Thus, while the Peak of Existence possesses the faculty of equanimity, it does not possess these latter three faculties. This concludes the commentary.
